title: Budget Law Preserved Key CHIP Safeguards While Cutting Medicaid and CHIP Spending
description_short: The July 2025 law retained CHIP bans on waiting periods, premium lockouts, and benefit caps, while making other Medicaid and CHIP cuts.
description_medium: President Trump signed H.R. 1 (P.L. 119-21) on July 4, 2025. The final law blocked many Medicaid and CHIP eligibility-rule provisions, but Georgetown’s post-enactment analysis says it left key protections for children in separate CHIP programs intact: waiting periods, missed-premium lockouts, and annual or lifetime benefit limits remained prohibited. The law made other Medicaid and CHIP cuts, so this correction distinguishes those effects from the CHIP barriers claimed in the frozen entry.
description_long: On July 4, 2025, President Donald Trump signed H.R. 1, the reconciliation law commonly called the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Georgetown University’s Center for Children and Families explains that although the final law blocked many elements of Medicaid and CHIP eligibility and enrollment rules, it left several child-specific protections in separate state CHIP programs unaffected. Waiting periods for otherwise eligible children, lockouts after a missed premium payment, and annual or lifetime dollar limits on CHIP benefits remained prohibited under the rule. The rule also required Medicaid and CHIP programs to coordinate eligibility decisions, transfer files when appropriate, accept one another’s determinations, and provide a combined household notice. These protections were already in effect or had a June 3, 2025 implementation date; the final law did not restore the barriers described in the original entry. This does not mean the law left Medicaid and CHIP unchanged. Georgetown’s CBO-based analysis estimated $990 billion in gross federal Medicaid and CHIP spending reductions over ten years and said those cuts account for 7.5 million of the increase in uninsured people projected for 2034. Those are projected effects of other provisions in the same law, not evidence for the original waiting-period claim.

source_fact_map.quote: several provisions that provide key protections for children in separate state CHIP programs which were instituted by the rule are unaffected by the law
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: While the budget reconciliation law blocks many elements of a two-part Medicaid and CHIP eligibility and enrollment rule finalized in September 2023 and April 2024, several provisions that provide key protections for children in separate state CHIP programs which were instituted by the rule are unaffected by the law. These provisions include: Prohibiting CHIP waiting periods. Under prior law, states were permitted to impose waiting periods of up to 90 days for children who are otherwise eligible for CHIP. Such waiting periods remain prohibited under the rule as of June 3, 2025. Prohibiting lockouts for missed premium payments. Under prior law, states could lock eligible children out of CHIP coverage for up to 90 days if their parents had previously missed a premium payment. Such lockouts remain prohibited under the rule as of June 3, 2025. Prohibiting annual or lifetime dollar limits on CHIP benefits. Under prior law, states were permitted to place annual or lifetime dollar limits on CHIP benefits if the overall value of CHIP coverage met CHIP standards. Any overall annual or lifetime dollar limits or dollar limits on individual CHIP-covered benefits remain prohibited under the rule as of June 3, 2025. Improving transitions between Medicaid and separate state CHIP programs. Under prior law, there could be coverage gaps if children enrolled in Medicaid instead became eligible for a separate CHIP program. Under the rule, as of June 3, 2024, in order to improve coverage transitions, state Medicaid and CHIP programs are required to make determinations of eligibility on behalf of the other program, transfer files when appropriate, and accept determinations made by the other program. Medicaid and separate CHIP programs are also required to provide a single, combined notice to all enrollees in the household.

children.title: Trump Directed DOJ to Investigate Allegations About Online Fundraising Platforms
children.description_short: On April 24, Trump directed DOJ and Treasury to investigate allegations about online fundraising platforms, with the memorandum citing ActBlue-related congressional findings. It did not establish wrongdoing.
children.description_medium: On April 24, 2025, President Donald Trump signed a memorandum directing the attorney general, in consultation with Treasury, to investigate allegations involving straw or foreign contributions through online fundraising platforms. The memorandum cited congressional findings involving ActBlue, and Reuters reported that the directive targeted ActBlue and other platforms. The sources document the order and its allegations, not criminal findings or proof of misconduct.
children.description_long: On April 24, 2025, President Donald Trump signed a memorandum directing the attorney general, in consultation with the Treasury secretary, to use lawful authority to investigate allegations that online fundraising platforms were used to make straw or foreign political contributions. The White House memorandum cited congressional findings about ActBlue and described suspected activity; it also directed the attorney general to report results within 180 days. Reuters reported that the memorandum targeted Democratic fundraising group ActBlue and other online platforms. The available sources establish the presidential directive and the allegations it cited. They do not establish that ActBlue committed a crime or that an investigation produced findings. This action occurred on April 24, not in early March. The original entry's assertion that DOJ simultaneously opened formal investigations of ActBlue and Open Society Foundations is not supported by this memorandum. Reporting about Open Society Foundations appeared months later and is represented in a separate child record. This description does not present the memo's allegations as proven facts.

children.title: DOJ Official Reportedly Asked Prosecutors to Prepare Plans to Investigate Open Society Foundations
children.description_short: September reporting said a senior DOJ official asked U.S. attorneys' offices to draft investigative plans concerning Open Society Foundations; it did not report findings or charges.
children.description_medium: On September 25, 2025, Reuters and The Hill reported that a Justice Department official had asked several U.S. attorneys' offices to prepare plans to investigate Open Society Foundations. The reports described a planning directive and possible charges under consideration, not a confirmed formal case, filed charges, or findings. OSF called the reported push politically motivated and said its work was lawful.
children.description_long: On September 25, 2025, Reuters reported that a senior Justice Department official had instructed several U.S. attorneys' offices to draft plans for an investigation of Open Society Foundations (OSF). The report, based on an earlier New York Times account, said the directive suggested possible charges, including arson and material support for terrorism. The Hill reported that an attorney in Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche's office sent a note asking prosecutors to prepare for investigations. These reports describe a request to prepare plans; they do not establish that prosecutors opened a formal case, filed charges, or found wrongdoing. Reuters said OSF described the reported push as politically motivated and stated that its activities were peaceful and lawful; that is OSF's response, not an adjudicated finding about motive. The date is late September 2025, months after Trump's April memorandum about online fundraising platforms. The supplied combined record placed the ActBlue and OSF matters together under an early-March date; available reporting supports treating this later reported directive as a separate event and correcting that timeline. No investigation outcome is established in the sources cited here.

title: Internal Draft: Supplied Allegation of a Second Joe Arpaio Pardon Remains Unverified
description_short: The supplied record alleges a second Jan. 20, 2025 pardon for Joe Arpaio; available official material does not establish the claim, so this draft is not for publication.
description_medium: The frozen entry alleges that President Trump issued former Arizona sheriff Joe Arpaio a second pardon on January 20, 2025. The supplied evidence instead points to the White House proclamation concerning offenses related to January 6 and a DOJ list of the president's 2025 clemency grants. Those pages were accessed, but they do not establish an Arpaio order. Keep the allegation internal and explicitly unverified until a specific pardon warrant or other reliable confirmation is found.
description_long: Internal draft; do not publish. The frozen entry alleges that President Donald Trump issued former Arizona sheriff Joe Arpaio a second pardon on January 20, 2025, covering the same conduct as an earlier pardon. That statement is retained only as an allegation from the supplied record. The cited White House proclamation is dated January 20 and concerns pardons and commutations for certain offenses relating to the events at or near the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021. The Department of Justice's public clemency page lists grants by President Trump beginning in 2025 and identifies that January 20 proclamation in its entry for that date. The accessed pages do not establish a second Arpaio pardon. Their scope does not prove that no separate order exists beyond the records reviewed, so this internal draft treats the central claim as unverified rather than disproven. The supplied record also says Trump pardoned Arpaio in 2017, but that history was not independently established from the sources accessed for this draft. Claims that a second pardon was mocked, legally unnecessary, politically motivated, or unprecedented are omitted because this packet provides no independent support for them. The January 20 date belongs to the allegation only; no 2025 Arpaio clemency event is asserted here.

title: DOJ Withdrew Eight OVW Grant Notices and Later Reopened Funding With New Terms
description_short: DOJ withdrew eight OVW grant notices in February 2025, then issued revised opportunities in May. The record documents a pause and reissue, not elimination of all OVW grants.
description_medium: On February 6, 2025, the Department of Justice's Office on Violence Against Women removed eight listed grant opportunities and told applicants that the notices were under revision. The 19th reported no updated funding notices until May 7, after the original deadlines; three months later, six new opportunities appeared, only two corresponding to the withdrawn set. DOJ later announced 19 FY2025 notices. This was a pause and revised release, not the elimination of every OVW grant.
description_long: On February 6, 2025, the Department of Justice's Office on Violence Against Women removed eight grant opportunities listed on its website and replaced them with a notice that applications were under revision. Reporting by The 19th, republished by Rewire News Group, said the office posted no updated funding notices until May 7, after the original application deadlines. Three months after the February removal, six new grant opportunities appeared, and only two were among those originally taken down. On May 23, the DOJ announced that OVW had released 19 notices of funding opportunity for FY2025 grants addressing domestic and dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking. The revised notices included changed priorities and restrictions. These facts support a record about a temporary withdrawal, delay, and revised grant release. They contradict the frozen entry's claim that the administration eliminated every OVW grant program in February and terminated more than $500 million in annual OVW funding. The cited reporting describes uncertainty for applicants, but does not establish that all survivor services ended, that shelters turned people away, or that the entire annual OVW budget was terminated. The corrected account keeps the reported pause and reissue distinct from unrelated DOJ grant cancellations.
